🧠 Cerebral Veins — Overview

  • Cerebral veins are devoid of valves (valveless) and run along the surface of the sulci.
  • They drain blood from the cortex and subcortical substance.
  • They terminate in the dural venous sinuses.
  • Divided into: Superficial cerebral veins and Deep cerebral veins.

A. Superficial Cerebral Veins

Drain into the superior sagittal sinus, and are known as bridging veins because they act as a bridge between the skull and the dural sinuses.

Mainly 3 veins: Superior — Middle — Inferior cerebral vein.

VeinAlternate NameDrains Into
Superior cerebral (anastomotic) veinVein of TrolardSuperior sagittal sinus
Superficial middle cerebral vein—Cavernous sinus / Sphenoparietal sinus
Inferior cerebral (anastomotic) veinVein of LabbéTransverse sinus

🧠 Mnemonic

Trolard Top (T,T) → Superior vein of Trolard.   Labbé Low → Inferior vein of Labbé.

B. Deep Cerebral Veins

Drain the deep subcortical structures: septal area, thalamus, basal nuclei.

1. Internal Cerebral Vein

Formed by the union of:

  • Septal vein — most medial
  • Thalamostriate vein — lateral
  • Terminal vein
Venous angle: the point where the septal vein and thalamostriate vein meet — it typically corresponds anatomically to the Foramen of Monro (between the lateral ventricle and third ventricle — each side has its own foramen).

2. Great Cerebral Vein (Vein of Galen)

Receives blood from the internal cerebral veins (after joining the basal vein of Rosenthal) and drains into the straight sinus.

Septal vein (medial)+ Thalamostriate vein (lateral)→ Venous angle→ Internal cerebral vein+ Basal vein→ Great cerebral vein (of Galen)+ Inferior sagittal sinus→ Straight sinus

🩸 Dural Venous Sinuses — The 10

They collect blood from the superficial and deep cerebral veins. The ten sinuses:

  • Superior sagittal sinus
  • Inferior sagittal sinus
  • Straight sinus
  • Left & Right transverse sinuses
  • Confluence of the sinuses
  • Sigmoid sinuses
  • Sphenoparietal sinus
  • Superior petrosal sinus
  • Inferior petrosal sinus
  • Cavernous sinus

Note: some pediatric patients may have an occipital sinus in the midline below the confluence of sinuses — a normal variant, not present in everyone.

Superior / Inferior Sagittal & Straight Sinus

Superior Sagittal Sinus

Extends from the foramen cecum to the internal occipital protuberance, and usually terminates in the right transverse sinus.

Receives blood from: superficial cerebral veins, diploic veins, emissary veins.

Inferior Sagittal Sinus

Courses in the inferior (free) edge of the falx cerebri (the dural reflection separating the two cerebral hemispheres).

Joins the great cerebral vein to form the straight sinus.

Straight Sinus

Formed by the junction of the great cerebral vein (of Galen) and the inferior sagittal sinus.

Terminates at the internal occipital protuberance, and usually drains into the left transverse sinus.

⭐⭐⭐ Venous Drainage Asymmetry (Crucial Radiology Hint)

When contrast dye is injected into the superior sagittal sinus, most of the flow favors the right transverse sinus.
Blood from the straight sinus predominantly favors the left transverse sinus.
The confluence of sinuses acts like a "roundabout" — important during cerebral angiography.

Transverse, Sigmoid & Sphenoparietal Sinuses

Left & Right Transverse Sinuses

Originate at the confluence of sinuses and course anterolaterally along the edge of the tentorium cerebelli (following the superior nuchal line) until reaching the mastoid bone, where they receive the superior petrosal sinus and become the sigmoid sinus.

Confluence of the Sinuses

Formed by the union of: superior sagittal + straight + (left & right) transverse sinuses.

Sigmoid Sinus

A continuation of the transverse sinus at the point where it joins the superior petrosal sinus, shaped like the letter S. Enters the jugular foramen to become the internal jugular vein.

Sphenoparietal Sinus

Lies along the lesser wing of the sphenoid bone, and drains into the cavernous sinus.

Cavernous Sinus

Surrounds the sella turcica (body of sphenoid bone) — located on either side of the pituitary gland.

LocationContents
Within the sinusInternal carotid artery + periarterial sympathetic plexus + Abducent nerve (CN VI)
Lateral wall (top to bottom)CN III (Oculomotor) → CN IV (Trochlear) → CN V1 (Ophthalmic) → CN V2 (Maxillary)

Receives blood from the superior & inferior ophthalmic veins and the sphenoparietal sinus, and drains via the superior petrosal sinus.

🚨 Clinical Pearl — The Danger Triangle of the Face

The area from the corner of the eye → corner of the nose → corner of the mouth is called the Danger Triangle. Squeezing a pimple or an infection in this area can travel retrogradely via the superior ophthalmic vein into the cavernous sinus, causing cavernous sinus thrombosis, which threatens the cranial nerves and the internal carotid artery.

Superior & Inferior Petrosal Sinuses

Superior Petrosal Sinus

Extends from the cavernous sinus to the junction of the transverse and sigmoid sinus (courses along the upper edge of the petrous bone). Receives tributaries from the pons, medulla, cerebellum, and inner ear.

Inferior Petrosal Sinus

Passes between the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) and the vagus nerve (CN X), then drains into the internal jugular vein after exiting the skull via the jugular foramen — it is the last tributary to join the jugular vein.

Also drains the cavernous sinus and the clival plexus (the venous plexus over the clivus bone — the posterior part of the sella turcica / anterior part of the foramen magnum).

🩺 Clinical Correlations

Subdural Hematoma — Bridging Veins

Laceration of the bridging veins (superficial cerebral veins) leads to subdural hemorrhage.

  • Most common in the elderly (60+ years) and more prevalent in men than women.
  • Most patients deny any history of trauma when a history is taken.
  • Cause: brain atrophy stretches the bridging veins like a taut string, so even minimal trauma (such as a sudden hard brake in a car) can shear these veins.
Click the image to enlarge 🔍

Cavernous Sinus Thrombosis (Danger Triangle)

See the Cavernous Sinus section above — infection spreading via the ophthalmic veins may reach the cavernous sinus and affect the cranial nerves (III, IV, V1, V2, VI) and the internal carotid artery.

⭐ High-Yield Exam Pearls

⭐⭐⭐ Must Know

  • Bridging veins = superficial cerebral veins → laceration → subdural hemorrhage.
  • Venous angle = Septal (medial) + Thalamostriate (lateral) veins ↔ location of Foramen of Monro.
  • Straight sinus = Great cerebral vein (of Galen) + Inferior sagittal sinus.
  • Within cavernous sinus: ICA + CN VI. Lateral wall (top→bottom): III, IV, V1, V2.

⭐⭐ High Yield

  • Right transverse sinus ← mainly from superior sagittal sinus.
  • Left transverse sinus ← mainly from straight sinus.
  • Sigmoid sinus → S-shaped → enters jugular foramen → internal jugular vein.
  • Last tributary to join the jugular vein = inferior petrosal sinus.
  • Occipital sinus = normal variant, more common in pediatric patients.

🧠 Mnemonics

Trolard Top (T,T) — superior anastomotic vein
Labbé Low — inferior anastomotic vein
